questions.q: Why does baking environment-specific configuration directly into a container image cause problems?
options: It forces a separate image to be built and tagged per environment, defeating the point of building an image once and promoting it unchanged
Container images are not allowed to contain any configuration files at all
Kubernetes refuses to run an image that contains hardcoded configuration
It makes the image larger than Kubernetes' maximum allowed size
questions.explain: Dev, staging, and production typically need different hostnames, flags, and keys. Hardcoding those into the image means rebuilding per environment, which breaks the build-once, promote-unchanged workflow images are meant to provide.

options: A YAML file that lives only on the kubectl client's local machine
A networking object that controls which Pods can reach the API server
A bucket of key-value pairs stored as a Kubernetes object, consumable by a Pod as environment variables or a mounted file
A special type of container image optimized for configuration data
questions.explain: A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive key-value configuration as a first-class cluster object, which a Pod can consume via envFrom/configMapRef or by mounting it as a volume.

questions.q: What does base64 encoding a Secret's values actually provide?
options: Full encryption, so the plaintext cannot be recovered even with cluster access
No cryptographic protection at all — it only makes binary-safe text for YAML storage; anyone who can read the Secret can decode it instantly
Automatic rotation of the credential on a schedule
A guarantee that kubectl describe will never display the value
questions.explain: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. kubectl get secret -o yaml plus a decoder returns the plaintext immediately — real protection comes from RBAC and encrypting etcd at rest, not from the encoding.

questions.q: In a Secret manifest, what does using `stringData` instead of `data` let you do?
options: Skip creating the Secret object entirely and inject values straight from the shell
Store the value unencoded in etcd, bypassing base64 altogether
Write the plaintext value directly in YAML and have Kubernetes base64-encode it automatically
Make the Secret visible in full through kubectl describe
questions.explain: stringData lets you author a manifest with readable plaintext values; Kubernetes base64-encodes them for storage on your behalf, same end result as using data with pre-encoded values.

questions.q: Which kubectl command actually reveals a Secret's base64-encoded value, as opposed to just its existence?
options: kubectl get secrets
kubectl describe secret web-app-db-credentials
kubectl get pods -l app=web-app
kubectl get secret web-app-db-credentials -o yaml
questions.explain: kubectl describe secret deliberately omits values, showing only byte counts. kubectl get secret -o yaml is where the base64-encoded data actually appears, which decodes instantly to plaintext.
